note_en: Earlier than the other two, it already reaches nearly maximum volume in the opening phrase. After catching its breath once, it hits the climax on that chord.
It plays each of the two halves only once, so it is much shorter than the other two. From the first beat it drives to the end at nearly maximum volume.
Starts the softest of the three. Its loud passages last the longest, and after pulling back once it rises to the climax.

headline_en: One build, no ups and downs
note_en: Has the least rise and fall of the three. It stacks up in one go from the start and reaches its climax the latest of the three.

headline_en: Shortest, loud from the first note
note_en: At 1 min 9 sec, it is 16 seconds shorter than Gilels. It enters loudly from the first note and reaches nearly maximum volume within 10 seconds.
Holds back the opening phrases, keeping them the softest of the three. It builds in one move at the middle and rings out loudly just once.

headline_en: Alone in peaking near the end
note_en: The other two press hardest around the middle, but this one alone presses hardest near the end.
Enters loudly from the start and pushes on to the middle without a break. The final phrase is set down much more softly than Seong-Jin Cho's.
At 1 min 25 sec, it is longer than the other two. It pulls back twice before the climax, then pushes on again.
At 34 seconds, it is the longest of the three. It presses hardest in the middle and sets down the ending the softest of the three.
After building once and pulling back, it reaches nearly maximum volume earlier than the other two. It also sustains the loud playing for a long time.
At 26 seconds, it is 6 to 8 seconds shorter than the other two. It sustains loud playing longer than Horowitz and Andsnes, and the ending hardly softens at all.
After building up, it pulls back deeper than Ashkenazy. Loud playing is brief, and it sets down soon after.
It takes both repeats yet finishes about 30 seconds sooner than Levit. On the repeats it plays evenly, at about the same volume as the first time.
Takes every repeat and plays the longest of the three. It stays even to the end and strikes loudest just before the final cadence.
Starts the softest of the three and grows bit by bit until the last quarter. At the end it steps down a level.
Enters at nearly maximum volume right at the start, and that level hardly drops until the end. It presses on as a single mass with no room to breathe.
Rings loudest in the first 10 seconds, then steps down a level and keeps the later part low. Its softest spot is also the deepest of the three.
Alone in starting from a soft sound, it rises to the full orchestra within 8 seconds. The time it sustains loud playing is the shortest of the three.
Drops to soft right after the climax and leaves it soft for the last 14 seconds. It sets down the soonest of the three.
Plays the first chord the hardest, then lets go sharply once in the middle. Before the end it climbs back to nearly maximum.
Sinks the second soft passage the lowest of the three. That makes the contrast the greatest when it surges again.
Plays the first third louder than the other two. It cuts back all at once in the middle, then climbs again.
Saves its strength for the first few seconds and builds bit by bit. The loudest sound bursts out 5 seconds before the end.
Rather than building in one go, it builds and releases phrase after phrase. After the climax it lets go the most of the three.
Builds from the very start and is almost at its loudest by about 10 seconds. It never comes down to the end, so it ends up the furthest from ‘soft’.

headline_en: Dips only a little in the middle
note_en: At 58 seconds, it is 6 seconds shorter than the other two. It sustains loud playing longer than the other two, and even the middle comes down only a little.

headline_en: A long stay at the top
note_en: Holds the third surge at maximum volume for almost 6 seconds. It sustains loud playing the longest of the three.
The flow is more even than in the other two. Near the end it reaches nearly maximum once more, and the close is also less soft.
The pattern of playing loudest after the figuration returns is the same as Kissin's. But the ending is much softer than Kissin's.
Alone in playing loudest in the opening section. From the middle it steps down a level, so its loud playing is shorter than the other two's.
The smallest difference in volume among the three, and it reaches nearly maximum the earliest. The ending also doesn't get as soft as in the other two.
At 3 min 30 sec, it is more than 30 seconds shorter than the other two. It already raises the volume to nearly maximum at the peak of the first melody.
Sings the first melody the softest of the three. Before the middle it sinks deeper still, and only just before the climax does it reach maximum.
At 4 min 17 sec, it is 47 seconds longer than Pollini. It doesn't lower the volume much from the first melody on, so the gap between soft and loud is smaller than in the other two.
Grows bit by bit toward the end, placing the loudest sound about 10 seconds before the finish. The ending is also less soft than in the other two.
The climax comes earlier than in the other two. After that it repeatedly drops deep, and ends the softest of the three.
At 2 min 58 sec, it is more than 15 seconds shorter than the other two. The gap in volume is also the smallest, and it pushes on evenly from start to finish.
Alone in playing loudest at the opening. After that it eases off bit by bit, leaving the ending very soft.
At 1 min 41 sec, it is the shortest of the three. It holds back at first and rises to its loudest at the very middle.
Unlike the other two, it puts the loudest sound in the first half of the piece. Ten seconds after the climax it sinks the deepest of the three.
At 2 minutes, it is longer than the other two, and its climax comes the latest. Twelve seconds after that it sinks deeply, then rises again.
Puts the climax late, then drops to the quietest point 10 seconds later. It finishes the ending much more softly than Lang Lang and Ott.
Puts the quietest sound at the opening and doesn't sink much afterward. The gap between soft and loud is also narrower than in the other two.

headline_en: Big again on the final return
note_en: After hitting the climax three quarters of the way through, it pulls back deeply once. On the final return it climbs back to nearly as loud.

headline_en: Eases back less after the climax
note_en: Rises to its loudest in the big middle passage. Even after the climax it eases back less than the other two, and it puts its softest point near the end.
After rising to its loudest in the middle, it sinks within 20 seconds to the lowest of the three. It also sustains loud playing longer than Perlman and Bell.
Starts the softest and ends the softest of the three. Before the climax it draws back deeply once, then rises in one move.
At 5 min 5 sec, it is about 30 seconds longer than the other two. After one big rise in the middle, it places the loudest sound in the later part.
At 6 min 20 sec, it is about 30 seconds longer than the other two. It keeps the loud playing the shortest of the three, and sets the ending down the softest too.
Alone in playing loudest in the middle. It sinks to the quietest point right after, setting the loudest and softest sounds close together.
Alone in placing the climax at the very end. Its first sound is also louder than in the other two, and it builds the final return big and sustains it to the end.

headline_en: Holds back until the last minute
note_en: At 4 min 10 sec, it is about 20 seconds longer than the other two. Only with a minute left does it reach nearly maximum for the first time.
At 8 min 8 sec, it is 47 seconds longer than Kleiber. It reaches nearly maximum only after almost 6 minutes.

headline_en: Maximum only at the very end
note_en: At 3 min 11 sec, it is the longest of the three. It lowers the middle the most, and reaches nearly maximum only in the last few seconds.

headline_en: Near maximum from the first tutti
note_en: Unlike the other two, it opens at nearly maximum from the first tutti. The gap between soft and loud is also the smallest of the three.
Keeps the first two thirds softer than Karajan and Ozawa. After dropping to its quietest, it climbs to the climax in 40 seconds.

headline_en: Near maximum only at the climax
note_en: The gap between soft and loud is the smallest of the three. It reaches nearly maximum for the first time only at the climax.
Reaches nearly maximum more than a minute earlier than the other two. Then it immediately cuts back to a very low level.
Drops the middle a level, then lifts the final 50 seconds again. Alone in placing the later part louder than the earlier part.
Drops to its quietest 20 seconds after the climax. But the ending stays less soft than in the other two.
Enters loudly from the start and reaches nearly maximum in 18 seconds. It sustains loud playing longer than Karajan and Muti.
Plays its loud passages shorter than the other two. Soon after the climax it sinks deep, and the later part continues a level lower.
Plays loudly in just one spot in the middle and sings far below that elsewhere. The final third sinks the softest of the three.
At 4 min 54 sec, it is more than a minute shorter than the other two. The gap in volume is also small, so it flows evenly from the start.
Starts the softest of the three. The gap between soft and loud is also the largest, and near the end it rises loudly once more.
Unlike Ashkenazy, it doesn't let the volume down even after the climax. Only on the last note does it drop to its quietest.
The ups and downs are slightly smaller than in the other two. The ending is set down as softly as Ashkenazy's.
At 4 min 32 sec, it is about 40 seconds shorter than the other two. It keeps the big middle passage loud for over a minute, and the ending doesn't get as soft as in the other two.
Rises loudly in two places and cuts back sharply between them. It ends the last 2 minutes very softly.
Rings the returning bells at maximum twice. It sustains loud playing the longest of the three.
Its first sound is the softest of the three. The gap between soft and loud is also the largest, and the flow is almost the same as Seong-Jin Cho's.
At 3 min 48 sec, it is about 30 seconds shorter than the other two. It starts getting louder the earliest, and closes the ending the least softly.
Holds back from the first bell more than the other two. Its loud playing comes only at the climax, and the gap between soft and loud is the largest.
Sings loudest at the one-third mark, the earliest of the three. It sinks the later part the deepest, so the volume gap is also the largest.
Forty seconds after the climax, it sinks to the lowest of the three. The last 10 seconds are also far softer than in the other two.

headline_en: A long sink, then one peak
note_en: Opens clearly for the first 20 seconds or so, then sinks for a long while. It sings loudly only once in the middle and sets down again.
Sinks the middle passage, which all three lower, the deepest. The loudest sound comes 1 min 15 sec before the end.
At 2 min 56 sec, it is 16 seconds longer than Lang Lang. It reaches nearly maximum in 35 seconds and sustains loud playing longer than the other two.
Unlike the other two, it puts the loudest sound on the final chord. It drops to its quietest 15 seconds before the end, then rises in one move.
Plays the first note softly, and reaches nearly maximum about a minute later than Levit. The climax also sits closer to the end than in the other two.
At 3 min 59 sec, it is the shortest of the three. It reaches nearly maximum in 15 seconds and sustains loud playing longer than the other two.
At 4 min 57 sec, it takes about a minute longer than Levit. Before the climax it sinks deeply once, then climbs again.
Plays loudest at the two-thirds mark of the piece, the earliest of the three. It also sustains loud playing the longest, and doesn't come down much even in the last 3 minutes.
Saves the loudest sound for the very last chord. About 2 minutes before the end it pulls back sharply, then builds up again.
Opens the introduction softer than the other two, and spreads the volume gap wider. The loudest sound comes in the coda.

headline_en: Held back until the final cry
note_en: Opens the beginning the softest of the three. It holds back until just before the final cry and reaches maximum there for the first time.
At 3 min 25 sec, it is longer than the other two. It places the first high point a level lower and builds steadily toward the final cry.
Already reaches nearly maximum at the first high point. The other two get that loud only at the final cry.
Pulls back a minute before the end, then builds again. The loudest sound comes well later than in the other two, 30 seconds before the end.

headline_en: Soft opening, loud in the middle
note_en: Plays the first note the softest of the three. The loudest sound comes a minute later than Pires, past the very middle.
At 4 min 6 sec, it is shorter than the other two. It barely changes volume from start to finish and keeps even.

headline_en: First call as loud as the last
note_en: Plays all four big passages at the same volume. Unlike the other two, it doesn't make the final chord louder.
Lowers the earlier big passages a level and plays loudest on the final chord. It also sustains loud playing the longest of the three.
facts_en: Academy of St Martin in the Fields

note_en: The flow is almost the same as Marriner's, putting weight on the final chord. But it cuts the loud playing shorter than the other two.
Starts louder than the other two and reaches nearly maximum in 26 seconds. Before the end it drops very low, then closes big again at the finish.
At 7 min 9 sec, it is about 40 seconds shorter than Trifonov. It doesn't lower the soft passages as deeply as the other two, and sustains loud playing the longest of the three.
Reaches the loudest sound only past the middle. The soft passage before the end sinks deeply earlier than in the other two.
The gap between soft and loud is the largest of the three. About a minute before the end it cuts back deeply, then rises near maximum again at the finish.
The climax comes later than Lisitsa's and Shishkin's. After that it drops the last minute a level, and the time spent on loud playing is also short.
At 8 min 4 sec, it is about 80 seconds shorter than the other two. It keeps the volume gap small, and reaches maximum earlier than both.

headline_en: All at once in the last 20 sec
note_en: Starts the softest of the three. After sinking once more in the middle, it builds up all at once in the last 20 seconds.

headline_en: At maximum through the second half
note_en: After catching its breath briefly twice early on, it drives the second half at nearly maximum volume.
As the ossia built on heavy chords, it is about 50 seconds longer than the other two. It enters loudly from the start and reaches maximum in 30 seconds.
At 3 min 16 sec, it is the longest of the five. It keeps the first part of the theme soft for a long time, then builds in three stages.
Just before the climax it pulls back sharply once, then rises in one move. The climb is the steepest of the five.
At 2 min 46 sec, it is the shortest of the five. It slashes in loudly from the first octave of the introduction and hits hard twice more in the theme.
The soft passage after the introduction lasts over a minute, the longest of the five. The climax also comes the latest.
Sings the first half at a similar, even volume. Its first note is the loudest of the four performances.
Enters the softest of the four. It is also the only one of the four to put the climax right in the middle.
At 1 min 13 sec, it is the shortest of the four. It cuts back deeply twice along the way, then climbs to its loudest at the end.

headline_en: A whisper for the first 4 sec
note_en: Keeps the first 4 seconds very quiet, then builds big within 20 seconds. The climax comes near the end of the piece.

headline_en: Maximum later than the other four
note_en: Reaches nearly maximum later than the other four. It sinks twice before the end, then surges again at the finish.
Sustains loud playing longer than the other four. Before the end it sinks the deepest, then bursts out again.
Passes quickly through the soft passage before the end. It plays the last 10 seconds the loudest of the five.
Enters more softly than the other four. It sinks for a long time twice before the end, and sets down the last bars the softest too.
Leaves the soft passage early and holds a level higher in volume for almost a minute until the climax.
Enters at nearly maximum from the first note. Even in soft passages it doesn't drop as low as Zimerman or Seong-Jin Cho.
Reaches nearly maximum a minute earlier than Marsalis and carries the first and second halves evenly. The loudest sound comes on the last chord.
Alone in playing loudest at the very middle of the movement. Before the end it sinks to its quietest, then rises again.
Reaches nearly maximum the latest of the three. It sinks the soft passages deeper each time, then cries out loudest on the final chord.
At 3 min 58 sec, it is longer than the other two. It keeps the middle minute a level lower, then rises again to play loudest.
Reaches nearly maximum the latest of the three, and that very spot is the climax. Before the end it drops to its quietest, then raises the volume again.

headline_en: Short, climax on the last chord
note_en: At 3 min 29 sec, it is about 30 seconds shorter than Högner. It holds loud playing for a long time, then plays the final chord the loudest.
Sinks the soft passage the deepest of the three. Even after the climax it sinks for a long while, then closes big at the end.
The flow is almost the same as Karajan's. But the softest spot is early in the movement, not after the climax.
The gap in volume is smaller than in the other two. The less it sinks, the longer it sustains loud playing.

headline_en: Climax in the middle of the piece
note_en: About 20 seconds longer than the other two, and alone in playing loudest in the middle of the piece. The ending isn't as big as the other two's.

headline_en: Up in a minute, then on to the end
note_en: Reaches nearly maximum the earliest of the three and sustains loud playing the longest. It carries that level to the end and puts the climax at the very end.
Starts more softly than the other two and builds toward the end. Before the end it sinks to its quietest, then cries out loudly at the very end.
Alone in placing the loudest sound in the final rush. During the 30 seconds of rushing, it hits nearly maximum again and again.

headline_en: Maximum in the middle and at the end
note_en: Raises both the middle and the final rush to nearly maximum. It sustains loud playing the longest of the three.
Rises loudest in the middle, and the final rush goes a level lower. The close is also softer than Gardiner's and Masur's.
Enters lower than the other two and holds back for almost a minute before surging. It doesn't sustain loud playing but cuts it short.
At 2 min 52 sec, it is the longest of the three. It reaches nearly maximum in 18 seconds and pushes on evenly with no big pull-backs.

headline_en: Near maximum from the first strike
note_en: Enters at nearly maximum from the first strike and, unlike the Emerson Quartet, sustains loud playing for a long time. It catches its breath once before the end, then drives on again.
At 1 min 58 sec, it is about 12 seconds shorter than the other two. It sinks the soft passages the deepest of the three, and sets down the ending the softest too.
Holds back the big passage in the first part more than the other two, reaching nearly maximum only after a minute. Its loud playing is also shorter than Serkin's.
Plays louder than the other two from the first note. It already rises to the climax's level early on, and builds to that level once more later.
At 3 min 9 sec, it is 27 seconds shorter than Gould. It reaches nearly maximum in 16 seconds and sustains loud playing for a long time.
At 3 min 36 sec, it is the longest of the three. It carries the middle louder than the other two, and rises to its loudest at the end.

headline_en: Built up in the last minute
note_en: Keeps loud playing shorter than the other two and stays a level lower until the middle. It builds big in the final minute or so.
At 7 min 38 sec, it is about a minute and a half longer than Yuja Wang. It sinks the soft passages the deepest, and ends the softest too.

headline_en: A level louder from the start
note_en: Opens the loudest of the three. Even after the climax it stays big for a while.
At 6 min 5 sec, it is shorter than the other two. The ending doesn't get as soft as Melnikov's.
Raises the orchestra to a big sound earlier than the other two. Afterward it doesn't sink as deep as the other two.
Opens the introduction the softest of the three, and it runs about 12 seconds longer than the other two. After holding back for over 30 seconds, it rises big in one move.
After the solo enters, it rises again louder than the other two. The ending also closes less softly than Bell's and Mutter's.
Plays the opening melody the softest of the three. So the contrast with the minor-key section is greater than in the other two.
At 1 min 31 sec, it is the shortest of the three. Through all three replies it keeps the loud level the most even of the three.
The other two are loudest at the first reply; only Lupu rises loudest at the very end. The middle is held a level lower.
At 8 min 29 sec, it is shorter than the other two. In the minor-key section it reaches nearly maximum four times, staying loud for over a minute.

headline_en: Loud even in the opening melody
note_en: Enters loudly from the first melody and reaches nearly maximum before the other two. It also opens the gap between soft and loud less.
Saves the first chord more than the other two, so reaching nearly maximum takes 18 seconds. It also sinks the middle the deepest.
After reaching nearly maximum on the first tutti, it sinks deeply on the second theme. The loudest sound comes later than in the other two, 4 seconds before the end.
Cries out the second fanfare louder than the first. It sinks the ending the softest of the three.
Reaches nearly maximum the earliest of the three and sustains loud playing the longest. After the second theme it rises big again and pushes on to the end.
At 1 min 45 sec, it is more than 15 seconds shorter than the other two. It cries out the first fanfare the loudest and answers the second at almost the same level.
At 2 min 10 sec, it is 25 seconds longer than Chailly. It cuts loud playing short and gives the soft passages more room toward the end.

headline_en: Big only in the last 20 seconds
note_en: Starts more softly than the other two and reaches nearly maximum only after more than a minute. It is also slightly longer than the other two.
At 1 min 31 sec, it is the longest of the three. It starts building about 10 seconds earlier than the other two and pushes the last 30 seconds loudly.
Plays the bassoon's first note softer than the other two. It builds bit by bit for over a minute, then raises it all at once 20 seconds before the end.
Opens the bassoon louder than the other two. It holds a similar level for over a minute, then builds in a rush in the last 20 seconds.
At 4 min 38 sec, it is more than 50 seconds shorter than the other two. It also sustains loud playing for the shortest time, and rises to its loudest near the end.
At 5 min 56 sec, it is more than a minute longer than Yundi Li. It sinks to its quietest in the later part, then rises to its loudest in 24 seconds.
Alone in rising loudest in the first fast section. It plays the returning fast section at almost that loud.
Plays the first note the loudest of the three, and the ending doesn't get as soft as in the other two. The gap between soft and loud is also narrower.

headline_en: Quietest a minute after the climax
note_en: At 5 min 1 sec, it is 41 seconds longer than Kissin. A minute after the climax it sinks to its quietest, and closes the ending more softly than Lang Lang and Kissin.
At 4 min 20 sec, it is shorter than the other two. It has already reached nearly maximum 15 seconds before the climax, and holds loud playing for a long time.
The loudest sound comes later than in the other two, in the later part. It sustains loud playing the longest of the three.

headline_en: Soft start, maximum at the end
note_en: At 9 min 25 sec, it is the longest of the three. It brings out the theme the softest and plays the final chord the loudest.
Opens the first sound more softly than the other two. It builds for over a minute and rises to its loudest just before the middle.
At 7 min 46 sec, it is about 1 min 40 sec shorter than Ciccolini. Alone in playing loudest in a middle variation.
Moves on evenly with no big pull-backs. It leaves the last 10 seconds louder than Litton and Chailly.

headline_en: Sinks before the end, then maximum
note_en: Like Ciccolini, it plays loudest at the end. About a minute before that, it sinks to its quietest and then pulls back up.

headline_en: Low until 20 sec from the end
note_en: Stays low for over a minute, then rises to its loudest in one move 20 seconds before the end. The gap between soft and loud is greater than in the other two.

headline_en: A level louder from the middle
note_en: At 1 min 36 sec, it is the longest of the three. From the middle section on it raises the volume a level and builds once more at the end.
Plays the clarinet's first note softer than the other two. It also presses the middle low, and rises in one move only at the very end.
Enters at nearly maximum from the first note and sustains loud playing the longest of the three. The middle drops only a level.
Opens the softest of the three. The gap between soft and loud is also the largest, and within a minute of the climax it sinks to its quietest.
At 3 min 15 sec, it is 22 seconds shorter than Giltburg. It catches its breath most deeply in the middle, and hits the climax earlier than the other two.
Carries the middle lower than Rubinstein. It reaches nearly maximum only with 40 seconds left.
Reaches nearly maximum earlier than the other two. It keeps the volume gap small and sustains loud playing for a long time.
At 6 min 52 sec, it is about 45 seconds longer than the other two. Alone in placing the climax past the 4-minute mark, and it sets down softly right after.
Keeps the first minute low. It starts getting louder later than the other two and builds all at once in the last 20 seconds.
Builds once earlier than Muti and Masur, then sinks deeply soon after. After that it builds up to the end in three stages.
At 1 min 53 sec, it is the shortest of the three. The first sound and the low point early on are both softer than in the other two.
Holds back the volume for over the first 30 seconds, then raises it slowly. It reaches nearly maximum the latest of the three, and its loud playing is the shortest too.

headline_en: Builds and lets go, again and again
note_en: Repeats building and letting go four times, rising a level each time. It plays loudest at the end, then cuts back sharply soon after.
Enters at nearly maximum from the first note and never lets down. It sustains loud playing the longest of the three.
At 1 min 49 sec, it is shorter than the other two. It keeps the first half a level lower, raises it in a rush later, and lets the ending down the most.
Pushes loudly from the start and reaches nearly maximum more than 40 seconds earlier than Bernstein. It also sustains loud playing longer than the other two.
After reaching nearly maximum in 6 seconds, it pulls back once, then rises to its loudest in the middle. The ending is also held big.
Alone of the three in reaching nearly maximum only in the big later passage. It sinks the theme the deepest and plays loudest there.
Alone in playing the first descending chord the loudest. It rises once more to almost the same level in the big later passage.

headline_en: Maximum at the start and later
note_en: Plays nearly maximum from the first descending chord. The loudest playing is in the big later passage.
Once it starts getting louder, it keeps a big volume to the end. Even after the climax it doesn't sink as much as the other two.
Sustains the loud opening exchange longer than the other two. After sinking, it leaves the ending less soft than Thibaudet does.
Places the climax later than the other two, then pulls back once and rises again. It closes the ending the softest of the three.
At 2 min 1 sec, it is about 15 seconds longer than the other two. After sinking deeply once, it rises to its loudest in the last few seconds.
At 1 min 46 sec, it is 15 seconds longer than the other two. It reaches nearly maximum in 4 seconds, and sinks the deepest later on.
Reaches nearly maximum the earliest of the three. It then sinks deeply and rises big again at the end.
The fastest of the three, so the surprise chord comes first. It lays the theme before it the softest, giving the greatest contrast.
Starts the softest of the three and keeps almost half very quiet. So the contrast when it rises big is the greatest.
Builds step by step from the opening and reaches nearly maximum earlier than the other two. Even after the climax it doesn't drop as low as Abbado and Böhm.
After building big in the middle, it lets down deeply to the end. The climax comes about 5 seconds later than in the other two.
Unlike the other two, it puts the loudest sound at the very end. After a soft passage, it rises in one move in the last 6 seconds.
At 1 min 43 sec, it is the slowest of the three. It begins the opening theme louder than the other two, and the surprise chord also comes the latest.
After the climax in the middle, it sinks the soft passage the lowest of the three. It sets down the ending more softly than Karajan and Marriner.
Reaches the climax 13 seconds earlier than Abbado and more than a minute earlier than Karajan. The soft passages go down only shallowly.
facts_en: Academy of St Martin in the Fields

note_en: Lays the opening theme as softly as Karajan does, and closes the final passage the loudest of the three.
facts_en: Academy of St Martin in the Fields

note_en: At 2 min 1 sec, it is about 20 seconds shorter than the other two. It puts the loudest sound past the very middle, later than Bell and Mutter.
At 2 min 21 sec, it is more than 15 seconds longer than the other two. Alone in playing loudest in the later part.
Starts more softly than the other two and plays loudest early on. It keeps loud playing the shortest of the three.
At 1 min 24 sec, it is the shortest of the three. It starts building at about 20 seconds, rises big early, and sustains loud playing the longest.

headline_en: Maximum from the first high point
note_en: Rises to nearly maximum from the first high point and sustains loud playing for a long time. The ending also closes bigger than in the other two.
Reaches nearly maximum 6 seconds earlier than Meyer and sustains loud playing for a long time. Near the end it rises big once more.
The first sound is louder than in the other two. After one big rise, it cuts back sharply in the middle, then rises again to play loudest.
Starts the softest of the three. The gap between soft and loud is also the largest, and it sinks deeply once more after the climax.
Keeps the first minute soft, and reaches nearly maximum only a few seconds before the end. Unlike Maisky, it saves its loud playing.
Brings out the first motif louder than the other two and reaches nearly maximum in 8 seconds. It also keeps loud playing going to the end.
Brings out the first motif the softest of the three. It puts the loudest sound in the middle, where Bernstein and Böhm put it at the end.
At 1 min 18 sec, it is the shortest of the three. It keeps the volume nearly even, rising big just once before coming right back.
After the tutti it sinks the soft passage deeper than Bernstein and Karajan. It holds loud playing for a shorter time than the other two.
At 1 min 41 sec, it is 23 seconds longer than Davis. It opens more softly than the other two, and sinks deeply once more before the climax.
The first sound is the loudest. From the beginning to the middle, and from the middle to the end, it thins out by almost the same amount.
Repeats small rises and falls three times, then rises big once. It sets the ending down more softly than the other two.
It cuts back sharply once in the middle, but leaves the later part the loudest of the three. The last 10 seconds are also the least soft.

headline_en: Builds for seconds, then the peak
note_en: Unlike the other two, it rings loudest after building for a few seconds. In the later part, contrary to Barenboim, it thins out to a very soft level.
Moves 25 seconds faster than Bernstein, yet sinks the ending deeper than the other two. It rings loudest within the first 13 seconds.
At 1 min 38 sec, it is the fastest of the three. It rings loudest within a few seconds of the first chord, and rebuilds the loud playing several times through the middle.
facts_en: Academy of St Martin in the Fields

headline_en: A leap at the second high point
note_en: Keeps the first high point the lowest of the three, then rises to maximum in one move at the second.
Sinks deeply right after the first chord. It builds again earlier than Fischer, holding the later passage a level higher.
Sinks the soft passage the most shallowly of the three. At the end it climbs back up to nearly the level of the first chord.
At 2 min 1 sec, it is more than 8 seconds longer than the other two. Unlike Bernstein, it holds the soft passage deep and long.
Drags 48 seconds longer than Marriner. Loud playing occurs only in the first minute, and the later part stays soft throughout.

headline_en: A few more seconds at the climax
note_en: The flow is almost the same as Karajan's. It doesn't let down right after the climax but keeps it big for a few more seconds.

headline_en: 2 min 14 sec, climax at the end
note_en: At 2 min 14 sec, it is 13 seconds longer than the other two. It holds back the early high point a level and puts the loudest sound at the end.
Enters at nearly maximum from the opening that the timpani begins. It sustains loud playing longer than the other two.
Builds step by step and plays loudest only after more than a minute. After the climax it sinks the softest of the three and ends there.
At 2 min 1 sec, it is 10 to 13 seconds shorter than the other two. The flow is the same as Ashkenazy's, rising to maximum all at once in the last 10 seconds.
Unlike Mutter, it keeps the volume gap small and builds evenly. Its loud playing is shorter than the other two's.
Plays the clarinet introduction the softest of the three. The gap between soft and loud is the largest, and it reaches maximum only in the last 10 seconds.
Opens the introduction less softly and reaches nearly maximum earlier than the other two. It then drives on loudly to the end.
The flow is almost the same as Rogé's. It builds a level at a time to the climax, and closes the ending less softly than Rogé does.
Opens the timpani's first strokes the softest of the three. The gap between soft and loud is also the largest.
At 1 min 52 sec, it is 9 seconds shorter than Mutter. It opens the timpani's first strokes loudly, the exact opposite of Mutter.
Reaches its climax the earliest of the three, then drops to its quietest right after, 9 seconds later. After that it repeatedly raises the volume big and lets it go.
The gap between soft and loud is narrower than Clara-Jumi Kang's and Mutter's. After the opening it moves evenly, with no big dips.

headline_en: Sinks, then a leap to the climax
note_en: Opens more softly than Clara-Jumi Kang and Perlman, and places the climax later. It drops to its quietest 11 seconds before the climax, then pulls up in one move.

headline_en: Hammer blow, then straight to soft
note_en: At 1 min 52 sec, it is the shortest of the three. It strikes at maximum from the first chord, then right away sets down to its quietest.
Alone in holding back the first chord, rising to maximum only after the repeated strikes. It builds bit by bit toward the end.
Starts more softly than the other two and grows without any big sinking. It saves the loudest sound for the final section.

headline_en: Loud even in the soft theme
note_en: Enters the loudest of the three. Even when returning to the soft theme, it doesn't come down as far as Perahia does.
Like Ashkenazy, it strikes at maximum from the first chord. Alone in placing the quietest sound near the end.
Plays loudest in the march section that appears first. Each time it returns to the theme it comes down deeply, separating it clearly from the march.
At 2 min 17 sec, it is 25 seconds longer than the Takács Quartet. It keeps the volume gap small and puts the loudest sound in the later part.
At 1 min 52 sec, it is the shortest of the three. It plays the two big rises at almost the same level.
Moves evenly with no big rises and falls, rising big only briefly near the end. Its loud playing is the shortest of the three.
Softer than the other two from the first note. It rises from its quietest point to maximum in 12 seconds, so the volume gap is also larger.
Rises big earlier than the other two, and holds that level until near the end.

headline_en: Sinks, then biggest at the end
note_en: Starts more softly than the other two. It sinks deeply once in the middle, then rises to its loudest at the end.

headline_en: A deep breath before the end
note_en: Carries the middle a level lower, and sinks deeper than the other two before the end. From there it rises again to the climax.
The first sound is the loudest of the three, and the volume gap is the smallest. Only near the end does it reach nearly maximum for the first time.
Starts less softly than Karajan and builds early. It reaches nearly maximum in a minute and sustains loud playing for a long time.
